title: Onsen Towns Near Tokyo: Which One Fits Your Trip
description: Hakone, Kusatsu, Kinugawa and Atami are all within a few hours of Tokyo, but they suit very different trips. Here is what each town is actually like, and who should pick which.
intro: If you have two weeks in Japan, you will probably want one night in an onsen town. The problem is that guidebooks list a dozen of them without saying how they differ — and they differ a lot. Hakone is a full day of sightseeing wrapped around a hot spring. Kusatsu is the water itself, strong enough that people go just for that. Atami is a seaside resort town you can reach in under an hour. Kinugawa is quiet, cheap, and close to Nikko's shrines. This guide sorts them by the kind of trip you are taking, not by ranking. Note that most traditional inns (ryokan) expect you to arrive by late afternoon and serve dinner early, so plan the day around checking in, not around checking out.
listHeading: Onsen towns within reach of Tokyo

buyingGuide.title: Decide whether the water or the town is the point
buyingGuide.body: Some onsen towns are destinations in themselves, with streets to walk, shrines to visit and things to see between baths. Others are essentially one very good hot spring with inns built around it. Hakone and Nikko/Kinugawa fall in the first group — you can fill a full day without ever getting in the water. Kusatsu leans toward the second: the town is small and the draw is the spring itself, which is among the most mineral-rich in the country. Ask yourself whether you want a sightseeing day that ends in a bath, or a trip where the bath is the entire plan.

buyingGuide.title: Check the travel time from central Tokyo honestly
buyingGuide.body: Travel time changes what the trip can be. Atami is roughly 40–50 minutes by Shinkansen from Tokyo Station, which makes an overnight trip easy and even a long day trip possible. Hakone is around 1.5–2 hours depending on the route. Kinugawa is about 2 hours by direct limited express from Asakusa. Kusatsu is the furthest, typically 3–4 hours by train plus bus. If you only have one free night, the extra hours each way matter more than the difference between the baths.

buyingGuide.title: Understand what a ryokan stay actually includes
buyingGuide.body: A traditional inn usually prices per person, not per room, and that price normally includes dinner and breakfast. This is why ryokan rates look high next to city hotels — you are booking two elaborate meals as well as the room. Check-in is often from 15:00 with dinner served around 18:00, and many inns ask you to be back by a set time. If you would rather eat in town or arrive late, look for a room-only plan or stay at a hotel in the same town instead.

buyingGuide.title: Know the tattoo situation before you book
buyingGuide.body: Many public baths in Japan still restrict guests with visible tattoos, and this catches a lot of overseas visitors by surprise. There are two reliable ways around it: book a room with its own private open-air bath (often listed as a room with kashikiri or private rotenburo), or choose an inn that explicitly states it is tattoo-friendly. Both exist in every town in this guide. Confirm on the property page before booking rather than on arrival — policies vary between inns in the same town.

places.name: Hakone
places.description: The default answer, and for good reason. Hakone packs an open-air sculpture museum, a lake with views of Mt. Fuji on clear days, a volcanic valley reachable by ropeway, and dozens of inns into one loop that is designed to be travelled by a single discounted pass. It is the easiest onsen town to visit without planning, which also makes it the busiest. Come here if you want your hot spring night to sit inside a full day of sightseeing.
pros: A full sightseeing loop — museums, lake, ropeway — not just baths
The widest range of inns, from budget to high-end
A single travel pass covers most local transport
cons: The most crowded of the four, especially at weekends
Mt. Fuji views depend entirely on the weather

places.name: Kusatsu
places.description: Kusatsu is where you go when the water is the reason for the trip. Its spring is highly acidic and strongly sulphurous, and the town is built around the yubatake — a wooden channel system in the centre of town where the hot water is cooled before it reaches the baths. It steams day and night and is lit after dark. The town is small and walkable, with free public baths dotted through it. Best for travellers who want the onsen experience concentrated rather than diluted with sightseeing.
pros: One of Japan's most distinctive and mineral-rich hot springs
The yubatake in the town centre is genuinely worth seeing at night
Compact and walkable, with several free public baths
cons: The longest journey of the four — hard to justify for one night
The strong sulphur water does not suit everyone

places.name: Atami
places.description: A seaside hot spring town on the Izu Peninsula that is close enough to Tokyo to reach before lunch. Atami is built up a steep bay, so most inns face the sea, and the town holds fireworks displays over the water several times a year rather than only in summer — unusual in Japan, and easy to plan a trip around. It feels more like a resort town than a traditional village. Best if your schedule is tight and you want sea views with your bath.
pros: By far the shortest journey — under an hour from Tokyo Station
Sea-facing inns and a bay setting
Fireworks are held across multiple seasons, not just summer
cons: More a modern resort town than a traditional onsen village
Sea views depend on which side of the building your room faces

places.name: Kinugawa Onsen
places.description: A river gorge lined with large hot spring hotels, and the practical choice if you are already going to Nikko to see Toshogu Shrine. Rates tend to be lower than Hakone for a comparable room, and several of the big hotels run all-you-can-eat buffet plans that work well for families. The town itself is quiet and past its bubble-era peak, which is part of the appeal if you want somewhere unhurried. Best as a second night attached to a Nikko trip rather than a destination on its own.
pros: Pairs naturally with Nikko's shrines and national park
Generally cheaper than Hakone for a similar standard of room
Buffet-style plans suit families and larger groups
cons: Little to do in the town itself after dark
Some hotels are dated compared with Hakone or Atami

faq.question: Can I visit an onsen town as a day trip from Tokyo?
faq.answer: Atami is the only one of these four that works comfortably as a day trip, at roughly 40–50 minutes each way by Shinkansen. Hakone is possible but rushed, and you would spend a large share of the day travelling. Kusatsu and Kinugawa are too far to be worthwhile in a single day. Note that most inns run their baths for overnight guests, though many towns also have public baths and day-use bathing at hotels, usually during limited afternoon hours.

faq.question: What if I have tattoos?
faq.answer: Many public baths still restrict guests with visible tattoos, so plan around it rather than hoping for the best. The two reliable options are booking a room with its own private open-air bath, or choosing an inn that states publicly that it is tattoo-friendly. Both are available in all four towns. Check the specific property's policy when you book — it varies between inns in the same town, and staff are unlikely to make an exception on arrival.

faq.question: Why are ryokan so expensive compared with hotels?
faq.answer: Traditional inns almost always price per person rather than per room, and the rate normally includes both dinner and breakfast — often a multi-course meal served in your room or a private dining room. So a rate that looks high against a city hotel is covering two substantial meals as well as the room. If you would rather eat in town, look for room-only plans, or stay at a regular hotel in the same onsen town and use its baths.

faq.question: When is the best time of year to go?
faq.answer: Autumn, roughly late October through November, is the most popular season, when the leaves turn and outdoor baths are at their best. Winter is quieter and there is a particular appeal to an open-air bath in cold weather. Avoid Japan's main domestic holiday periods — New Year, Golden Week in early May, and mid-August — when prices rise sharply and rooms sell out months ahead. Book well in advance if your dates fall near a weekend in autumn.
